title: The Unofficial ATSA Prep Guide & Practice Pack
description: Structured prep system for the FAA ATSA skill sections: what the test is, the test-day playbook including the Num Lock trap, the collision-section method with the scan-name-decide-act drill, memory chunking for numbers and differences, mnemonic body-mapping for equations with variables, spatial-visual and logical-reasoning methods, the consistency-over-perfection personality rule, a three-to-four-week prep plan with diagnosis profiles, the post-test score timeline, the retake playbook, honest verified pricing across the prep market, plus a 18-pair grounded QA bank, five checklists, three decision trees and a provenance-stamped fact layer with explicit verification notes. Unofficial, not affiliated with the FAA.

sections.title: Part 1: How to Use This Guide
sections.content:
This is a structured preparation system for the skill sections of the FAA Air Traffic Skills Assessment (ATSA), the computer test taken at a Pearson VUE center as the second step of the air traffic controller hiring process. It is built from what real test-takers report, not from official FAA materials, because the FAA publishes almost nothing about the test. Claims that come from candidate reports rather than verified sources are flagged with a how-to-check note; a full verification appendix collects them.
The honest version of what this guide can and cannot do: it can make the sections concrete, give a practice method, and remove the walking-in-blind anxiety that dominates the evidence threads. It cannot predict a score, and no product can. The test measures aptitude under pressure; the best prep makes sure the right skills are practiced, not that the test has been memorized.
This product is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or officially connected to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) or the Air Traffic Skills Assessment (ATSA). ATSA is a trademark of the FAA. All practice content is independently developed; it is a training aid, not a copy of the official test.

sections.title: Part 2: The Complaint Map
sections.content: The guide opens with the recorded pain of real candidates, each mapped to the chapter that solves it. I walked out so upset because I was convinced I bombed it, then scored Well Qualified and now work at a facility: the score is a black box for weeks and anxiety is part of the test, solved in the post-test chapter. Nobody actually knows what they did wrong, the entire process is unknown to the public: no feedback after failing means you must prep differently blind, solved in the retake chapter. The collision section was hard and my biggest problem was pressing all clear and then realizing two dots would collide much later: collision judgment under time pressure is the core skill, solved in the collision chapter. Is the memory test really going to give me like six seconds to read and memorize all those, I am averaging fifty percent or less: memory pacing feels impossible without a system, solved in the memory chapters. If I am being honest about myself it could look bad, but if I answer what they look for my answers seem unnatural: the personality section punishes gaming, solved in the personality chapter. It is ninety-nine dollars for one month and eighty-nine for one week, does anyone think it is still worth it: prep pricing is absurd and the affordable middle is missing, solved in the pricing chapter. If you do not pass it this time you will have to wait months before this bid comes up again: one shot per bid makes retakes scarce, solved in the prep and retake chapters. I had a few mess-ups because I fat-fingered the num lock key on the pad: test-day logistics steal points, solved in the test-day chapter.

sections.title: Part 3: What the ATSA Actually Is
sections.content:
The ATSA is a computer-based test taken in person at a Pearson VUE testing center. It is free of charge. The commonly reported structure is seven sections over roughly two hours fifty minutes, with up to thirty minutes of break time that can be divided as needed. The exact section count and order vary by report; the pointSixtyFive ATSA Compilation thread is the canonical community breakdown and should be checked for the current consensus.
The sections that matter: Memory Test 1, Numbers and Differences, where a number appears and a mental operation such as a difference between displayed values is performed under tight pacing. Memory Test 2, Equations with Variables, where an equation with variables flashes for a few seconds and a value must be solved from memory; candidates consistently report roughly six seconds per flash. The ATC Radar Simulation or collision section, where aircraft appear as numbered circles on a radar screen and the candidate presses the number key of a circle about to collide to remove it, or presses zero when the sector is safe; this is the section candidates describe as the hardest. Spatial-visual relationships, logical reasoning, word problems and reading comprehension, which are standard aptitude material with an ATC flavor including charts, ranked orders, seating arrangements and pattern logic. Finally the personality inventory, typically a large forced-choice battery of over one hundred questions in a most or least style, where there are no right answers and consistency is the scored dimension.
The test feels like a black box because the FAA does not publish scoring weights, pass thresholds or per-section feedback. Candidates report waiting weeks for a single email that says Well Qualified, Qualified or Not Qualified with no breakdown. That is by design; managing the uncertainty is part of the aptitude being measured.

sections.title: Part 4: Test-Day Playbook: The Cheap Points
sections.content:
The evidence threads are full of preventable losses that cost nothing to fix. Keyboard map: the collision section uses the number pad; know where every key is before sitting down, with one through nine for aircraft numbers and zero for sector safe. Practice on a number pad rather than the top row, because muscle memory is the whole game.
The Num Lock trap: multiple candidates report accidentally hitting Num Lock mid-section and losing responses. Whether a testing center keyboard locks Num Lock on is center-dependent; ask the proctor before the section starts or test a key on the pad in the tutorial, and glance at the Num Lock light between rounds.
Plastic key covers or keypad stickers can provide tactile insurance so pad keys are distinguishable without looking, but Pearson centers have rules about what may be brought; check the testing center allowed-items policy and ask the proctor when in doubt.
Proctor rules: candidates report being told they must be completely quiet, with no whispering answers even quietly. Practice silently at home and assume no talking, no phone, no notes and no leaving the room without permission.
Breaks: up to thirty minutes total, dividable. Candidates recommend a short break between the memory sections and the collision section, the two highest-pressure blocks. Drink water, stand up, reset, and use the bathroom during a break rather than during a section.
What to bring: government-issued ID matching the application is the consistent requirement. Current FAA and Pearson requirements change; check the confirmation email received when scheduling.

sections.title: Part 5: The Collision Section: Judgment Under Pressure
sections.content:
This is the section candidates describe as the hardest and where prep diverges most from the real test. The evidence is consistent: the real test feels denser and faster than practice materials, and the clear timing is unforgiving. It measures conflict detection under divided attention: can you watch multiple converging aircraft, identify which pairs will actually collide, and act before it is too late while the radar keeps moving.
The core method is decide, act, then recover. Scan for converging pairs first; two circles on intersecting paths with similar speed are the danger, while parallel or separating pairs are safe. Prioritize collisions over anything else; multiple candidates report the same lesson that when there is a choice between doing math and saving a plane, save the plane, because the collision is the catastrophic failure and a skipped math question costs one answer. Use the no-collision call deliberately; pressing zero when the sector is safe is a real decision, not a default, and candidates report the failure mode of pressing zero and then watching two dots converge because the lookahead is longer than it feels. When in doubt about a pair, ask whether they will be within touching distance while still on screen; if yes, remove one. After a collision, recover rather than melt down; real takers report surviving four to ten collisions and still scoring Well Qualified, though the FAA does not publish the collision tolerance. One collision is not a failed section; the next aircraft still needs your eyes.
A concrete scan drill: run one round with a single rule, naming the converging pair out loud before pressing anything. Saying it forces the eyes to find the pair before the thumb acts, which is the exact order the real test rewards. Then run a round where only zero is pressed, building the safe-sector call into a reflex, then combine scan, name, decide, act. Ten minutes of that sequence beats an hour of passive watching because the test measures the decision loop, not familiarity with radar graphics.

sections.title: Part 6: Memory Test 1: Numbers and Differences
sections.content:
The reported challenge is tight pacing, a mental operation on a flashed number, and no feedback on whether the answer was right until it is over. The method is to chunk and operate.
Read the number as chunks rather than digits; eight four seven two becomes eighty-four seventy-two or eight, four-seven, two depending on what the operation needs. Chunking is how working memory holds more and is the same trick used for phone numbers.
Do the operation immediately in the head, silently because whispering is not allowed on test day. The difference between two flashed numbers should become a reflex: subtract the smaller from the larger, hold the result, type it.
Never confuse the last number shown with the answer. This is the exact failure candidates report, where the typed answer feels like the number just seen. Say the answer to yourself once before typing so the label sticks.
Miss one, reset. Candidates report the resilience rule that if you lose the thread, drop it and start fresh from the next number; one lost answer is not the section, a spiral is.
Practice protocol: ten minutes a day with a flash-and-recall tool. The free simulator companion to this guide has a memory section and any digit-flash app works. Two-second exposure per item, immediate recall, no feedback until the round ends, mirroring real conditions.

sections.title: Part 7: Memory Test 2: Equations with Variables
sections.content:
Candidates consistently report the same shock: a multi-variable equation flashes for what feels like six seconds, then vanishes, and a value must be solved from memory. The method is mnemonic mapping.
Assign variables to physical anchors. The community's most reported system is body mapping, where A is thumb, B is index and C is middle finger, storing each variable's value on the corresponding finger. Mnemonic systems are candidate-reported technique rather than FAA endorsed, but the underlying principle of spatial encoding is standard memory research.
Read the equation as a sentence rather than symbols. A plus B minus C with values anchored to fingers becomes a tiny physical sequence of thumb plus index minus middle; you recall the motion rather than the symbols.
Do the arithmetic in the same order every time. Fix a sequence such as left to right or parentheses first and never vary it, because under time pressure the procedure is the memory.
Whisper rules: on test day you cannot whisper, so practice solving entirely silently with finger positions as the only external aid. If you find yourself needing to say it aloud at home, you are still depending on the wrong channel and should fix that before test day.
Practice protocol: six-second flash, immediate solve, no feedback until the round ends. Five minutes a day beats thirty minutes once a week because the skill is retrieval speed, and retrieval speed is built in short frequent sessions.

sections.title: Part 8: Spatial-Visual Relationships
sections.content:
The reported shape is pattern-completion and spatial reasoning items with an ATC flavor at a one to two second per item pace, with style details varying by report and the pointSixtyFive compilation describing the section.
The method: the eye-reversal rule. Candidates report the classic trap that the correct answer is often the mirror or rotation of the obvious one; if an option looks like the pattern but reversed, check whether the reversal is the intended answer. This is a candidate-reported heuristic.
Warm up before the section. The first few items set the pace, so do two or three deliberately slowly to calibrate then accelerate. The evidence threads describe candidates finding their rhythm mid-section, which is lost points.
One to two seconds per item maximum. The pace is the test. When you hesitate past the rhythm, guess and move on; a wrong answer on one item is cheaper than losing the section's pacing.

sections.title: Part 9: Logical Reasoning, Word Problems and Reading Comprehension
sections.content:
The reported shapes are seating arrangements, ranked orders, charts and passage-based questions with ATC context.
The method: draw the arrangement. Seating and ranking questions are solved on paper or in the scratch space by drawing the table, writing the order and filling from the constraints; never hold it in your head.
Ranked-order traps: the classic error is answering who is second when the question asked who is last, or the reverse. Circle the question word before reading the options.
Chart questions: read the axes first. Determine what is being measured, in what units and over what period; candidates report losing points by answering from the chart's shape rather than its labels.
Reading comprehension: passage first, question second, evidence third. Skim the passage, read the question, then find the sentence that answers it. The answer must trace to a sentence rather than to an inference about the topic.

sections.title: Part 10: The Personality Section: Consistency Beats Perfection
sections.content:
This is the section candidates understand least, and the evidence threads show why: it feels like it should be gameable, and the reports say gaming it backfires.
Candidates report a large forced-choice battery, roughly one hundred or more questions, choosing the response that is most like you and least like you across repeated dimensions. There are no objectively correct answers, and the exact question count and format come from candidate reports.
The trap: if I am honest, my answers might look bad, but if I answer what they want it looks unnatural. The reported consequence of strategizing is inconsistency. Repeated questions are the same construct asked different ways; if you answer what you think they want each time, your answers stop matching each other, and the inconsistency is the signal.
The method is to be consistent rather than perfect. Answer as yourself with first instinct, because the first response that feels true is the one you will repeat consistently; the strategic answer changes by question while the true one does not. Watch the forced-choice mechanics; most and least batteries force a pick between the stronger and weaker of two traits, so pick the one that is more true and move on, because agonizing burns time and produces answers that drift. Understand the liars signal; candidates report and the community consensus holds that people who try to project a perfect profile score worse because the inconsistency shows up, though there is no official confirmation. The safest strategy is the one that needs no memory: be yourself, every time. If you took the test before and answered differently the second time, the exact failure one three-time taker reported, that is the mechanism; same person, same answers, every attempt.

sections.title: Part 11: The Three to Four Week Prep Plan
sections.content:
The typical window from application to test day is roughly three to four weeks, depending on the bid, so check the confirmation email. Candidates who fail consistently report either under-preparing by walking in blind or over-preparing with weeks of expensive prep that did not match the real test. This plan is the middle: daily, short, section-true.
Week one, diagnose. Days one and two, take one full-length practice pass using the free simulator or the ten dollar app to find weak sections; do not study yet, measure. Days three through five, thirty minutes per day on the two weakest sections, which for most people are collision and memory. Days six and seven, repeat the diagnosis; the sections that moved are where time goes.
How to read the diagnosis: most candidates land in one of three profiles. The collision-heavy profile, collision accuracy under sixty percent while memory holds, needs scan drills first with fewer aircraft and slower closing speeds and deliberate safe-versus-converging calls, then density up. The memory-heavy profile, digits and variables bleeding together, needs chunking and mnemonic work before any timing pressure: get the recall method solid at your own pace, then add the flash timer. The pace profile, everything roughly correct but too slow, needs the one to two second rhythm drills: force the decision, accept the wrong answers, build the tempo. Identifying the profile in week one makes weeks two and three efficient instead of busy.
Week two, method. Forty-five minutes per day alternating collision drills, memory drills for numbers and variables, and one full mixed session, using the mnemonic systems every session until automatic. Sunday, a full timed run scored and compared to week one.
Week three, simulate. Forty-five to sixty minutes per day, but every session is timed, silent and section-sequenced like the real test: memory, spatial, collision, with a short break. Practice the keyboard map blind with hands on the pad and eyes on the screen. One full-length simulation mid-week and one on Sunday.
Week four, rehearse. Taper to thirty minutes per day with review only in the last two days; do not learn new material in the final forty-eight hours. The day before: logistics check of ID, center address, arrival time and what to bring, light practice and sleep. The evidence threads are full of people who lost points to fatigue and logistics rather than ability.
The overstudying warning: the thread about studying three weeks with JobTestPrep and still getting Not Qualified is the cautionary tale that prep which does not match the test's pressure does not transfer. The point of this plan is pressure-matched practice, not volume.

sections.title: Part 12: After the Test: The Silence, Decoded
sections.content:
Candidates report weeks of silence after the test, then a single email with a rating; reported timelines vary by bid and two to six weeks is the expected range.
The ratings: Well Qualified is the strongest band, Qualified is the mid band, and Not Qualified or Not Referred means the bid's bar was not cleared. The FAA's exact referral bands and their current meaning are published in the job announcement, which is the authoritative source for a given bid.
What the I-thought-I-bombed-it phenomenon means: a striking share of the evidence threads are people who walked out certain they failed and then got Well Qualified. The test is designed so you do not know how you did; the uncertainty is the experience. Do not read your performance in the room as your score; wait for the email.
What to do while waiting: nothing changes the score. Rest, apply to the next bid when it opens, and keep the prep light so a retake, if needed, starts from a warm baseline rather than cold.

sections.title: Part 13: Failed? The Retake Playbook
sections.content:
The reality candidates report: you cannot retake the ATSA until the next bid opens, and bids come in waves months apart. The bid cadence changes, so check the FAA hiring announcement calendar. This is the scarcity that makes each attempt expensive, and it is also why a structured retake plan matters.
What you can know: the email gives a rating band and nothing else. The FAA does not tell you which section failed, what your score was, or how close you came, and no official per-section feedback is published.
What the evidence says about retakers: the three-time taker reports Well Qualified on the first attempt and Qualified on the next two, and thought they failed every time; the score does not move the way people expect. One retaker's reported cause of regression was answering the personality section differently the second time; consistency is a scored dimension, so changing answers between attempts changes the profile. Retakers who improve report doing the same core method work on collision and memory, not buying more prep.
The retake plan: first, do not buy new prep to fix a diagnosis you do not have. The no-feedback problem means more of the same materials will not tell you more; the affordable tools cover the same sections as the ninety-nine dollar platforms, and the difference is practice design, not content volume. Second, rebuild from the fundamentals; collision scanning and memory chunking are the two skills that dominate candidate reports, and six weeks of daily twenty-minute drills on those two beats any cram. Third, reapply on the next bid with the same consistent answers: same method, same personality answers, same prep routine, removing every variable you control so the test measures the aptitude rather than the variance you introduced.

sections.title: Part 14: The Honest Pricing Chapter
sections.content:
The market, verified in August 2026: JobTestPrep ATSA PrepPack is seventy-nine to ninety-nine dollars with one week to three month tiers, though exact tiers differ between a candidate report of eighty-nine dollars for one week and ninety-nine for one month and a listing review of seventy-nine for one week, eighty-nine for one month and ninety-nine for three months. ATC Preparation ATSA Preparation Suite is fifty-nine ninety-nine for a thirty-day recurring subscription. Prepopedia Complete ATSA Practice is forty-nine dollars one-time with three-month unlimited access, snippet-verified. Peterson's AT-SA Exam Prep is fifty-nine dollars per month recurring, snippet-verified. The ATSAPro app is roughly ten dollars one-time. Free tiers exist from ATC Preparation Level 1, 123atc, and browser simulators at zero dollars.
What the expensive tiers actually buy is repetition volume, section-mapped question banks and, on the highest tiers, multiple full-length practice tests. That is real value if used. The evidence thread's honest summary: one candidate skipped the ninety-nine dollar pack, just tried looking to see what to expect, and scored Well Qualified. Another called the ninety-nine dollar pack not worth at all and recommended the ten dollar app for the basics.
The honest recommendation: this guide, the free simulator companion and one cheap full-length practice pass cover the same sections as the ninety-nine dollar platforms at a fraction of the cost, if the daily drills are actually done. The thing expensive tiers cannot buy is pressure-matched practice; that is a habit, not a product. If a full-length simulation beyond the free one is wanted, the ten dollar app or a single month of a mid-tier platform is the reasonable add, not the ninety-nine dollar subscription used for two weeks.

qa_bank.question: How long is the ATSA and how many sections does it have?
qa_bank.answer: The commonly reported structure is seven sections over roughly two hours fifty minutes at a Pearson VUE center, with up to thirty minutes of dividable break time. The exact count and order vary by report, so check the pointSixtyFive ATSA Compilation thread for current consensus.

qa_bank.question: Is the ATSA free to take?
qa_bank.answer: Yes, the ATSA itself is free of charge; you take it in person at a Pearson VUE testing center. The cost is in prep materials, which range from free simulators to ninety-nine dollar platforms.

qa_bank.question: How does the collision section work?
qa_bank.answer: Aircraft appear as numbered circles on a radar screen. You press the number key of a circle about to collide to remove it, or press zero when the sector is safe. It measures conflict detection under divided attention and is the section candidates describe as hardest.

qa_bank.question: What is the core decision rule in the collision section?
qa_bank.answer: Prioritize collisions over anything else. When there is a choice between doing math and saving a plane, save the plane: the collision is the catastrophic failure and a skipped math question costs one answer.

qa_bank.question: How many collisions can you survive and still score Well Qualified?
qa_bank.answer: Real takers report surviving four to ten collisions and still scoring Well Qualified, but the FAA does not publish the collision tolerance. Treat that range as directional rumor, not specification, and treat every collision as expensive but not fatal.
qa_bank.provenance: candidate reports only; not officially published

qa_bank.question: What is the Num Lock trap?
qa_bank.answer: Multiple candidates report accidentally hitting Num Lock mid-collision-section and losing responses. Whether the testing center keyboard locks Num Lock on is center-dependent; ask the proctor before the section starts or test a key in the tutorial, and glance at the Num Lock light between rounds.

qa_bank.question: How do you handle the memory flash timing?
qa_bank.answer: Chunk the number into groups rather than individual digits, do the operation immediately and silently, and never confuse the last number shown with your answer. Miss one, reset, and start fresh from the next number rather than spiraling.

qa_bank.question: What mnemonic system do candidates use for the variable equations?
qa_bank.answer: Body mapping: assign variables to physical anchors such as A as thumb, B as index and C as middle finger, storing each variable's value on the corresponding finger. Read the equation as a sentence and do the arithmetic in the same order every time.

qa_bank.question: Should you try to game the personality section?
qa_bank.answer: No. The reported consequence of strategizing is inconsistency: repeated questions are the same construct asked different ways, and answering what you think they want each time makes your answers stop matching each other. Answer as yourself with first instinct, every time, on every attempt.
qa_bank.provenance: candidate reports; community consensus, not official

qa_bank.question: What do WQ, Q and NR mean?
qa_bank.answer: Well Qualified is the strongest band, Qualified is the mid band, and Not Qualified or Not Referred means the bid's bar was not cleared. The FAA's exact referral bands and their current meaning are published in the job announcement you applied under.

qa_bank.question: Why do people think they failed when they actually passed?
qa_bank.answer: The test is designed so you do not know how you did; the uncertainty is the experience. A striking share of evidence threads are people who walked out certain they failed and then scored Well Qualified. Do not read your in-room performance as your score; wait for the email.

qa_bank.question: How long do you wait for ATSA results?
qa_bank.answer: Candidates report weeks of silence, then a single email with a rating. Reported timelines vary by bid, with two to six weeks the expected range. Nothing you do while waiting changes the score.

qa_bank.question: What should you do differently on a retake?
qa_bank.answer: Do not buy new prep to fix a diagnosis you do not have; the affordable tools cover the same sections as the expensive platforms. Rebuild the two fundamentals, collision scanning and memory chunking, with daily short drills, and reapply with the same consistent answers on every attempt.

qa_bank.question: Can you change your personality answers between attempts?
qa_bank.answer: You can, but you should not. Consistency is a scored dimension; one retaker's reported cause of regression was answering the personality section differently the second time. Same person, same answers, every attempt.

qa_bank.question: Is the ninety-nine dollar prep worth it?
qa_bank.answer: One candidate skipped it, practiced with the ten dollar app, and scored Well Qualified; another called it not worth at all. The expensive tiers buy repetition volume and full-length tests, which is real value if used. The guide plus a free simulator plus one cheap full-length pass covers the same sections if the daily drills are done.

qa_bank.question: What is the one-to-two second pace rule?
qa_bank.answer: In the spatial-visual section the pace is the test: one to two seconds per item maximum. When you hesitate past the rhythm, guess and move on, because a wrong answer on one item is cheaper than losing the section's pacing.

qa_bank.question: How do you solve seating and ranking questions?
qa_bank.answer: Draw the arrangement: draw the table, write the order and fill from the constraints in the scratch space. Never hold it in your head, and circle the question word before reading the options to avoid the second-versus-last trap.

qa_bank.question: What is the three-week prep structure?
qa_bank.answer: Week one diagnose with a full practice pass and thirty minutes a day on weak sections. Week two method with forty-five minutes a day alternating collision and memory drills plus a Sunday timed run. Week three simulate with timed silent section-sequenced sessions and two full-length runs. Week four taper to thirty minutes review only.

checklists.title: Test-Day Checklist
items: Government-issued ID matching your application
Confirmation email with center address and arrival time
Number pad location memorized: 1-9 aircraft, 0 sector safe
Ask proctor about Num Lock behavior before the section
Test a pad key in the tutorial to confirm keyboard state
Plastic key covers or stickers if allowed by center policy
Silent practice: no whispering, no talking, no phone, no notes
Break plan: short reset between memory and collision sections
Use the bathroom during a break, not during a section
Arrive early enough to be calm, not rushed

checklists.title: Week 1 Diagnosis Checklist
items: Days 1-2: one full-length practice pass, no studying yet
Record per-section accuracy to find the weak sections
Days 3-5: thirty minutes daily on the two weakest sections
Days 6-7: repeat the practice pass and compare sections
Identify profile: collision-heavy, memory-heavy, or pace
Collision-heavy: scan drills, fewer aircraft, deliberate calls
Memory-heavy: chunking and mnemonics before any timing
Pace profile: one-to-two-second rhythm drills, accept wrong answers

checklists.title: Collision Scan Drill
items: Round 1: name the converging pair out loud before pressing
Round 2: press only zero, no diversions, build the safe-sector call
Round 3: combine scan, name, decide, act
Prioritize collisions over math when both demand attention
After a collision: recover, do not melt down, next aircraft needs your eyes
Ten minutes of this sequence per session, not passive watching

checklists.title: Memory Method Checklist
items: Read numbers as chunks, not individual digits
Do the operation immediately and silently
Say the answer to yourself once before typing
Never confuse the last number shown with your answer
Miss one, reset: drop it and start fresh from the next number
Variables: assign A, B, C to fingers or body anchors
Read equations as sentences, recall the motion not the symbols
Same arithmetic order every time
Practice entirely silent, no whispering even at home

checklists.title: Retake Plan Checklist
items: Do not buy new prep to fix a diagnosis you do not have
Rebuild the two fundamentals: collision scanning and memory chunking
Six weeks of daily twenty-minute drills on those two skills
Same method, same personality answers, same prep routine as last attempt
Remove every variable you control before test day
Check the next bid window on the FAA hiring announcement calendar
Expect no per-section feedback; plan blind and prepare for pressure
